articleTitle: Services provided by the international satellite consortia
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Liberalisation in the Provision of Satellite Services
abstract: Discusses how satellite communications networks involve major capital investments. This fact, together with the need for a complete global coverage in order to provide full international telecommunications facilities has led to the formation of a number of major international satellite consortia. The largest of these is Intelsat, which currently has 116 member countries from around the world. Intelsat satellites provide fixed satellite services, such as voice, data and television, both on a point-to-point and point-to-multipoint distribution basis, between telecommunications operators and users all around the world.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Practical problems of implementing a satellite distribution system
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Liberalisation in the Provision of Satellite Services
abstract: To fully appreciate the range of uplink services that are going to be provided by Satellite Information Services (SIS) it is worth examining the services that SIS provide in 1989. In 1986 the change in the legislation allowed television into betting shops for the first time, this led to the possibility of a new integrated television and communications package for the betting industry. Satellite emerged as the most effective method of transmission. SIS was set up to develop the project for the benefit of the entire betting industry.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Liberalisation of satellite services-a DTI view
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Liberalisation in the Provision of Satellite Services
abstract: In June 1988 it was announced that 27 applications for specialised satellite service (SSS) licences had been received, and in October it was announced that, after due consideration, these licences were to be awarded to: British Aerospace; British Satellite Broadcasting; Electronic Data Systems; Maxwell Satellite Communications; Satellite Information Services; and Uplink. Also Kingston Communications would be permitted to operate fixed uplinks from within the Hull area, and to run transportable uplinks within the rest of the country. The author discusses the nature of the services, frequency usage and coordination of Earth stations, possible further liberalisation and an outlook to the future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Telecommunications liberalisation and regulation in the United Kingdom
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Liberalisation in the Provision of Satellite Services
abstract: The whole thrust of telecommunications policy in the UK has been towards liberalisation and competition. The author discusses the steps that are being taken to introduce competition in satellite services and the role that Oftel plays as regulator. He deals with three aspects: the liberalisation of specialised satellite services, Oftel's ruling on PanAmSat and the impact of separate satellite systems. Finally, he looks at what the future might hold for users and providers of satellite services.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Using satellites to help people make a bigger profit
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Liberalisation in the Provision of Satellite Services
abstract: Discusses how when OTS2 went up in the 1970s, the prospect of a pan-European satellite system began to look possible, and people in the UK and Europe started talking about using satellites for business purposes, as well as telecommunications. The author presents ideas and proposals for the use of satellite systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Liberalisation-the view point of the manufacturer (satellite communications)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Liberalisation in the Provision of Satellite Services
abstract: Discusses how for a liberalised Europe to succeed in the field of satellite communications there has to be a harmonisation of policy, technical standards and commercial procedures which accept liberalisation as good for the customer, operator and manufacturer. At present the customer wants liberalisation by which they interpret as being able to operate their own satellite system, the operator does not want liberalisation by which they interpret as losing their market and the manufacture is squeezed leaving the market open to non European competitors from areas of the world where the rules are more clearly defined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
